Spotted tilapia (Pelmatolapia mariae) attains a maximum recorded body size of 39.4 centimeters [Li = 39.4 centimeters] in total length, a measurement derived from field surveys of adults in West African river systems. This ultimate length places the species among the larger-bodied tilapias, with individuals frequently exceeding the sizes typical of congeneric cichlids occupying similar lacustrine habitats. The value represents the asymptotic dimension approached by fish that have completed their somatic growth trajectory, generally observable in specimens older than several years. During routine sampling conducted in the Nyong River basin, researchers documented several individuals approaching this length, confirming that the species can achieve considerable size under favorable environmental conditions. The observed growth pattern suggests a prolonged period of mass increase, with fish continuing to add length well beyond the onset of reproductive activity. This ultimate total length serves as a key reference point for constructing length-weight relationships and estimating fecundity parameters in population models.

Sexual maturation in this cichlid occurs when individuals reach a total length of 15 centimeters [Lp = 15 centimeters], a benchmark that marks the transition from the juvenile stage to a reproductively viable state. This length at puberty represents the threshold at which gonadal recrudescence begins, typically coinciding with the onset of vitellogenesis in females and spermiation in males. Field data from Lake Maracaibo indicate that most individuals achieve this length within their first year of life, though local thermal regimes can influence the precise timing. Once this size is attained, adults weighing approximately 54.5 grams [Wwp = approximately 54.5 grams] initiate breeding activities, investing resources toward gamete production and nest construction. The corresponding body mass at this developmental milestone was derived from a length-weight conversion, reflecting the typical condition factor of wild populations. This coordinated transition in both length and mass ensures that individuals are sufficiently large to successfully defend territories and produce viable offspring in competitive environments.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant water temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C], spawning females produce clutches of approximately 18 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 18 eggs per spawning event], with individual females exhibiting high repetitive spawning activity. These reproductively active adults typically complete approximately 0.5 spawning events per day [F_R_i = approximately 0.5 spawning events per day], sustaining this elevated reproductive tempo over extended periods. The maximum reproductive output documented at this thermal regime underscores the species capacity for rapid population increase under favorable conditions. Each clutch is deposited on prepared substrate, after which both parents engage in extended brood care, fanning and guarding the developing embryos until they become free-swimming larvae. This pattern of high fecundity and parental investment allows the species to colonize new habitats efficiently. The 23 °C [T = 23 °C] temperature approximates the mean annual water temperature in the species native range, providing a realistic baseline for laboratory-based life-history studies.

Newly hatched yolk-sac larvae emerge from demersal adhesive eggs measuring approximately 2.5 millimeters in diameter, and these prolarvae initially weigh about 0.0082 grams [Wwb = about 0.0082 grams] wet weight at birth. This extremely small birth mass reflects the modest energy reserves contained within the fertilized ovum, which sustains the larva during the endotrophic phase before the mouth opens and first exogenous feeding commences. The larval period is brief, with yolk-sac resorption occurring within a few days after hatching, at which point the young fish must begin capturing prey. During this critical transition, mortality can be substantial if suitable microzooplankton are not readily available. The small size at emergence constrains the initial trophic niche, limiting first-feeding fry to rotifers and small nauplii. As the juveniles grow, they rapidly expand their dietary range, incorporating larger invertebrates and detrital material. This early life-history strategy, characterized by high fecundity and small offspring, is typical of many iteroparous cichlids inhabiting productive tropical waters.

Maximum longevity for Spotted tilapia has been estimated at 4,745 days [am = 4,745 days] under stable laboratory conditions maintained at 23 °C [T = 23 °C], representing approximately 13 years of potential lifespan. This substantial duration places the species among the longer-lived members of the cichlid family, with senescent declines in reproductive output and somatic condition typically observable only after the tenth year. At this advanced age, the asymptotic adult weight of approximately 978.7 grams [Wwi = approximately 978.7 grams] reflects the substantial biomass accumulation possible over an extended lifetime, with larger individuals often dominating hierarchical social structures within breeding aggregations. The relationship between longevity and large body size in this species aligns with broader life-history theory predictions for tropical freshwater fishes, where stable thermal environments favor slower senescence rates. Continued monitoring of marked populations in both natural and captive settings will further refine our understanding of age-related physiological changes in this ecologically important cichlid.
